questions.question: What does the index set $T$ do in a stochastic process?
options: It is the set of values each $X_t$ can take
It is the sample space on which each $X_t$ is defined
It must be a finite set of observation times
It labels the random variables in the family

questions.question: What is a sample path?
options: The distribution of $X_t$ at one fixed index $t$
One realization of the process across the index set
The set of all possible realizations of the process
The average of many realizations at each index $t$

questions.question: The number of arrivals up to time $t$ in a queue is what kind of process?
options: A discrete-time stochastic process
A single random variable with integer values
A continuous-time stochastic process
A deterministic counting function of $t$

questions.question: Why must the random variables be on a common probability space?
options: So every $X_t$ has the same marginal distribution.
So the variables $X_t$ are independent of each other.
So all the $X_t$ take values in one common set.
So joint behavior across indices is meaningful.

questions.question: Which description matches the definition of a stochastic process $\{X_t\colon t\in T\}$?
options: Random variables $X_t$, one per index $t$, all on one common probability space
A single random variable whose value changes as the time $t$ moves on
One realised path $t\mapsto x_t$, a fixed number for each index $t$
A list of marginal distributions, one per index $t$, with no joint model

questions.question: In a process, each of $X_5$ and $X_6$ equals $1$ or $0$ with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$ each. Nothing else about the process is given. What can you say about $\mathbb{P}(X_5=1\text{ and }X_6=1)$?
options: It equals $\tfrac{1}{4}$, the product of the two marginals
It equals $\tfrac{1}{2}$, the common marginal probability
It is not determined; any value in $[0,\tfrac{1}{2}]$ is possible
It is not determined, but it lies strictly between $0$ and $\tfrac{1}{2}$

questions.question: A process $\{X_t\colon t=0,1,\ldots,10\}$ starts at $X_0=0$; at each step its value moves up or down by $1$, and every sequence of ten up- and down-steps is possible. Let $R$ be the event that the path reaches level $4$ at some time $t\le10$. How is $R$ related to the event $\{X_{10}\ge4\}$?
options: $R=\{X_{10}\ge4\}$, since a path that reaches $4$ stays at level $4$ or above
$R\subseteq\{X_{10}\ge4\}$, and some paths with $X_{10}\ge4$ never visit $4$
$R$ is not an event, since it involves many indices $t$ at once
$\{X_{10}\ge4\}\subseteq R$, and some paths in $R$ have $X_{10}<4$
